title: Tell HN: Stop using MLX, start telling your agent to write custom kernels
text: I am one of the many people who started clustering Macs for local AI. At first, it seemed amazing, but that was before the huge agentic revolution. No one could put up with 10 tok/sec after a 15 minute wait, in hermes agent. I asked claude to build a kernel, and boy it did deliver. Across four Macs, Baidu ERNIE 5.5 flash preview was running 96 tok/sec at low context. In hermes, running nearly 50 tok/sec at high context, only a fifteen second wait for a response. title: Ask HN: Nobel Prizes for OpenAI and Anthropic: When?
text:
In 2024, multiple Nobel Prizes were awarded for AI related accomplishments:

> 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics: Awarded to John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for foundational discoveries and inventions enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks.

(Source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton)

> 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Awarded to Demis Hassabis and John M. Jumper for developing an AI algorithm (AlphaFold) that predicts complex three-dimensional protein structures

(Source https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02527-z)

I would classify the work that got them the physics prize as basic research that played a big part in enabling AI. And the prize in Chemistry falls into a similar category I think…

Now, both openAI + Anthropic are maybe less involved in basic research directly but the things they "produce" are now used to solve problems humanity tried to solve for many many years. If they both published all of their papers under a different name, a name that sounds like a real persons name, I am sure that person would be considered for multiple Nobel Prizes.

It rarely happens but "organizations" can receive Nobel Prizes. Eg.:

> The European Union (EU) won the 2012 Nobel Peace Prize for over six decades of advancing peace, reconciliation, democracy, and human rights in Europe

So why not OpenAI + Anthropic? (Yes, its maybe still a bit early, given that some of the papers still are pending proper peer review - but overall the question remains: How would humanity deal with "that"? "That" being that the "products" of two companies made those scientific breakthroughs?

title: Re: Show HN: Modelpin – see what changes when your LLM...
text:
Hi HN! Im Samartha, a student from Bengaluru and I've been working on Modelpin during my free time mostly in the evenings.

The problem that i'm trying to solve: AI providers ultimately retire their old/previous models on a particular date, and the replacement model doesn't always behave the same way like the previous model did. So, the tests you conduct on the codebase with the new model might still pass because the final text/result looks correct, but the model is doing something different underneath the hood, like calling different tools.

So I built Modelpin which is a CLI. You describe a few scenarios regarding your app or codebase. It records how your current model behaves and then it replays the same scenarios on the new or the replacement model, and tells you what exactly changed. It runs each scenario multiple times for both models. A difference between them only counts if it's statistically significant, big enough to matter, and shows up again on a fresh set of runs, so normal model randomness doesn't get reported as a change. And there's also 'modelpin watch', which tells you which models in your config are about to retire, along with the vendor's date and page it came from.

It runs locally on your computer or in your CI with your API key. It works with Anthropic, Gemini, OpenAI(chat completions) and its compatible hosts. It's licensed as Apache 2.0. You can try an offline demo without any keys. It takes few commands:

  pip install modelpin
  modelpin init --demo
  cd modelpin-demo
  modelpin baseline --fixtures traces.json
  modelpin check --to demo-model-v2 --fixtures traces.json
Why its the high time? : Anthropic has plans to retire Sonnet 4.5 soon(30 November, tentative), and they recommend sonnet 5.5 instead. I tested that switch on a small customer-support bot I wrote for the test: 8 scenarios, 6 tools, and 10 recorded runs of Sonnet 4.5 per scenario.

What I found: A customer asks for the neighbour's address based on the neighbour's delivery order and Sonnet 4.5 declined all the runs without calling for any tool. Whereas Sonnet 5.5 looked up the neighbour's order first and then declined, in all 120 runs that I have full records of, on the original prompt. Nothing errored, and no reply leaked the address, so a check that only looks up for the final output would pass. But there was this one extra tool call that would have gone unnoticed.

I tried 3 prompts, and the third rewrote the rules as steps in order, and with it there was no regression in 30 repeat checks across Sonnet 5.5, 5 and 4.6. I didn't test which part of that change fixed it. Method, scenarios and counts are here: https://gist.github.com/samarthputhraya/e2795f9ef6e70fef8ec3...

What it doesn't do: It only measures scenarios you give it and can miss subtle changes. The judge that compares meaning is a model too, and Modelpin doesn't measure quality; it measures change. It won't tell you whether the new model is better or not. It also doesn't switch models or open PRs for you.

Feedback I'd like to have: does the scenario setup make sense for a real app, what do you check today before switching models, and is anything in the output confusing?

title: Show HN: Pintura – YAML Slides for agents to edit and humans to review
text:
Pintura is designed for AI agents to work on plaintext files and for humans to review in a browser.

The premise is that when you're doing slides with AI agents, you mainly need to review their work and iterate until you're happy.

The main benefits are: 1. You can use git for version control and clear diffs. 2. The browser UI is designed for review: flip between versions with visual changes highlighted, pin comments, or drag/reword directly. 3. Your agent gets a CLI that helps it catch things like text overflow, misaligned elements, hanging words, etc.

It pairs with our spreadsheet companion Libreta (github.com/editide/libreta) if you want to link numbers. Clicking a linked number on a slide pops up a spreadsheet showing the formula or a screenshot of the original source.

I've been using this to build financial decks from the terminal with Claude Code (and now Antigravity). It's much nicer than flipping back and forth between Excel and PowerPoint. Here are some decks I've built with this setup: https://iterativaresearch.com/

Everything (preview, checks, screenshots, HTML/PDF export) is Apache-2.0 and runs locally with no account. PowerPoint export currently runs through our API with a free plan.

title: Show HN: Animama – Open-source AI desktop companion with 3D avatars
text:
Hey HN, I'm Raymond, a long-time reader of the site.

For the past year I've been working on Animama, a free and open-source (AGPL) AI desktop companion with 3D anime-style avatars.

A quick rundown of the Anima (AI companion) features:

- Personality: an IDENTITY.md file you can edit

- Memories: a memory filesystem of Markdown files. Animas have tools to read and write these files, and you can edit them too

- Emotions: Animas can express 24 emotions, which drive their facial expressions, tone of voice and behavior

- Behavior: 300+ gestures and reactions, built on a custom JSON animation format (animaPoseClip)

- Structured output: every reply is text plus an emotion and a gesture, which the avatar acts out as it speaks

You bring your own API key. The low-cost models from OpenAI (GPT-6 Luna) and Anthropic (Claude Haiku 5.5) are good enough, so a few dollars of usage goes a long way. Local models are supported but still experimental.

When I started, pretty much all human-AI interaction was typing into a chat box and getting a wall of text back. I felt this could be made more engaging, interactive and fun. Like everything else in AI, things have improved a lot since then. We now have speech-to-speech models (GPT Live, Gemini Realtime), and even the frontier labs have released their own AI avatars (Codex pets, Grok's Ani). Animama is just one solo developer's take on it.

My original idea was an AI productivity companion (think Clippy, RIP), and it still kind of is. But it's obviously never going to compete with the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps, so I leaned more into the character side of things.

Anyways, I built this because I thought it would be a fun project. But, it did make me realize that there are some serious risks to AI Companion apps, so I've made the app 18+ with safety guardrails built in (e.g. an Anima admits it's an AI if you sincerely ask).

Three ways to try it:

1. Desktop app (Apple silicon Mac, Windows 11, linux and windows 10 coming soon): https://animama.ai/download

2. Self-host with Docker: see the README

3. Web demo: sign up at https://animama.ai

Docs: https://docs.animama.ai

Happy to answer any questions!
